stem: A company uses scripts to stop development instances every evening and start them each morning.
prompt: Which cloud economics benefit does this demonstrate?

options.text: Data transfer becomes free for stopped instances
options.why: Data transfer pricing has nothing to do with stopping instances.

options.text: Automation reduces cost by running resources only when needed
options.why: Stopping idle instances outside working hours cuts compute charges.

options.text: Reserved capacity lowers the cost of idle instances
options.why: Reserved capacity charges whether instances run or not.

options.text: Economies of scale reduce the hourly rate
options.why: The hourly rate stays the same; savings come from running fewer hours.

explanation.answer: On-demand resources are billed while running, so automatically stopping them when unused saves money.
explanation.concept: Automation is a cost lever: schedule, scale and clean up resources without manual effort.
explanation.examTip: Turn off what you don't use (automatically) = lower bill.

stem: A company compares running PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 with using Amazon RDS. The EC2 instance price is lower than the RDS price for the same size.
prompt: Why might Amazon RDS still have a lower total cost?

options.text: Amazon RDS includes unlimited free storage
options.why: RDS storage is billed separately; it is not unlimited or free.

options.text: EC2 instances are billed per request instead of per hour
options.why: EC2 is billed by time, not per request, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: RDS removes staff time for patching, backups and failover
options.why: The managed service takes over tasks that would cost engineering time on EC2.

options.text: Amazon RDS backups are included without any limit
options.why: Backup storage beyond the free allocation is billed.

explanation.answer: Total cost includes labor. Amazon RDS automates patching, backups and Multi-AZ failover, which reduces operational effort.
explanation.concept: Compare total cost of ownership, not only the hourly price of the resource.
explanation.examTip: Hourly price isn't everything: managed services save staff time.

stem: A small company worries it cannot afford the physical security, such as guards and biometric access, that large data centers have.
prompt: How does moving to AWS help with this concern?

options.text: Physical security is unnecessary in the cloud
options.why: Physical security is essential; AWS provides it.

options.text: Customers must hire their own guards for AWS data centers
options.why: AWS is responsible for physical security of its data centers.

options.text: AWS lets customers visit data centers to check security
options.why: AWS does not allow customer tours; it shares third-party audit reports instead.

options.text: AWS secures the physical data centers for all customers
options.why: Physical security is AWS's responsibility under the shared responsibility model.

explanation.answer: AWS is responsible for the physical security of its facilities, so every customer benefits from enterprise-grade protection.
explanation.concept: Under the shared responsibility model, AWS secures the cloud (facilities, hardware, network); customers secure what they put in it.
explanation.examTip: Physical data center security = AWS's job.

stem: A company runs fault-tolerant batch jobs that can stop and restart at any time without harm.
prompt: Which cloud economics idea lets it run these jobs at the lowest compute cost?

options.text: Use spare capacity at steep discounts (Spot Instances)
options.why: Spot Instances use spare EC2 capacity at large discounts and suit interruptible work.

options.text: Use the largest On-Demand instances available
options.why: On-Demand pricing is the most expensive per hour of these options.

options.text: Commit to three years of fixed capacity
options.why: Long commitments discount steady workloads but lock in spending.

options.text: Buy dedicated hardware for exclusive use
options.why: Dedicated hardware costs more, not less.

explanation.answer: Spot Instances offer spare EC2 capacity at discounts of up to 90% compared with On-Demand. They can be interrupted, so they fit flexible, fault-tolerant work.
explanation.concept: Matching pricing models to workload characteristics is a key cloud economics skill.
explanation.examTip: Interruptible + flexible = Spot.

stem: A company's on-premises disaster recovery site sits idle most of the year but still costs as much as the primary site.
prompt: How can AWS reduce this cost?

options.text: Use larger EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone
options.why: This does not provide disaster recovery and adds cost.

options.text: Keep a minimal copy in AWS and scale it up only during a disaster
options.why: Pay-as-you-go lets the company pay little until it actually needs to recover.

options.text: Run a full copy of production in a second Region at all times
options.why: A fully running copy costs about the same as the idle DR site.

options.text: Store disaster recovery backups only on the primary site
options.why: Backups on the primary site would be lost in the same disaster.

explanation.answer: AWS lets you run only the minimum for disaster recovery (for example pilot light) and scale up on demand, instead of paying for an idle duplicate site.
explanation.concept: Disaster recovery strategies trade cost against recovery time.
explanation.examTip: Idle DR site = keep a small copy on AWS and scale when needed.

references.title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud

stem: A student wants to learn AWS without spending money and asks if anything can be tried for free.
prompt: Which AWS offering helps?

options.text: Dedicated Hosts
options.why: Dedicated Hosts are paid physical servers.

options.text: Savings Plans
options.why: Savings Plans lower prices for a usage commitment; they are not free.

options.text: AWS Free Tier
options.why: The AWS Free Tier lets new customers try many services at no charge within set limits.

options.text: AWS Enterprise Support
options.why: Enterprise Support is a paid support plan.

explanation.answer: The AWS Free Tier provides free use of many services within limits, so learners can explore without cost.
explanation.concept: Free Tier usage beyond limits is billed, so set up AWS Budgets alerts.
explanation.examTip: Try AWS at no charge = Free Tier (watch the limits).

stem: A company signs a five-year data center lease, then moves everything to AWS after two years.
prompt: Which statement BEST describes the financial effect?

options.text: The company immediately saves the full cost of the lease
options.why: The lease is a fixed commitment that the company may still have to pay.

options.text: AWS costs replace lease costs one for one, so the bill stays flat
options.why: The company may pay both for a time, which is a change.

options.text: AWS reimburses data center lease costs for migrations
options.why: AWS does not reimburse customers' lease costs.

options.text: The lease is a sunk fixed cost that may overlap with AWS costs
options.why: Fixed commitments made earlier can overlap with new variable costs during the transition.

explanation.answer: Fixed costs such as leases continue regardless of usage. Migration plans often account for overlapping costs until commitments end.
explanation.concept: This is why the cloud's shift to variable costs is valuable: fewer long-term fixed commitments.
explanation.examTip: Existing leases and contracts are sunk costs; factor them into migration timing.

stem: A developer wants to run code in response to events without provisioning or managing any servers and without paying for idle time.
prompt: Which approach fits BEST?

options.text: Use AWS Lambda functions
options.why: Lambda runs code on demand, manages the servers and bills only for the compute time used.

options.text: Use a Dedicated Host
options.why: Dedicated Hosts are physical servers you pay for continuously.

options.text: Run code in an on-premises virtual machine
options.why: On-premises VMs require managing hardware and are paid for even when idle.

options.text: Run code on a long-lived EC2 instance
options.why: An EC2 instance must be managed and is billed while idle.

explanation.answer: AWS Lambda is serverless compute: AWS manages the infrastructure and you pay for requests and compute duration.
explanation.concept: Serverless removes server management and idle costs for event-driven workloads.
explanation.examTip: Code without servers, pay per use = Lambda.

stem: A website's database is overloaded because the same product pages are requested millions of times a day.
prompt: Which design approach reduces the database load the MOST?

options.text: Add more columns to the product table
options.why: Schema changes do not reduce the number of reads.

options.text: Cache frequently read data close to the application
options.why: A cache such as Amazon ElastiCache serves repeated reads without hitting the database.

options.text: Move the database to a larger instance every week
options.why: Ever-larger instances raise costs without addressing repeated reads.

options.text: Delete old product records more often
options.why: Deleting records doesn't reduce repeated reads of popular pages.

explanation.answer: Caching stores frequently accessed data in memory, reducing load on the database and improving response time.
explanation.concept: Caching layers include Amazon ElastiCache for application data and Amazon CloudFront for web content.
explanation.examTip: Same data read again and again = cache it.

stem: A manager asks what an Availability Zone is.
prompt: Which description is correct?

options.text: A content cache location used by CloudFront
options.why: That describes an edge location, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: A country where AWS stores customer data
options.why: Countries can contain Regions, but an AZ is a set of data centers within a Region.

options.text: Isolated data centers with redundant power in a Region
options.why: Each AZ is isolated from failures in other AZs and connected with low-latency links.

options.text: A single server rack inside one data center
options.why: An AZ is much larger than a rack, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking and connectivity in an AWS Region.
explanation.concept: AZs in a Region are physically separated but connected with low-latency networking.
explanation.examTip: AZ = isolated data center(s) within a Region.

stem: A company wants to bring software licenses that are tied to physical CPU sockets and cores, and its vendor requires visibility into the physical server.
prompt: Which EC2 option meets this requirement?

options.text: Spot Instances
options.why: Spot Instances run on shared capacity and can be interrupted; they do not expose physical cores.

options.text: Default shared tenancy On-Demand Instances
options.why: Shared tenancy does not give physical server visibility.

options.text: AWS Lambda
options.why: Lambda abstracts servers entirely, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Dedicated Hosts
options.why: Dedicated Hosts give visibility into sockets and physical cores, supporting per-socket or per-core licenses.

explanation.answer: Dedicated Hosts are physical servers dedicated to you, with visibility of sockets and cores for bring-your-own-license compliance.
explanation.concept: Dedicated Instances run on dedicated hardware too but do not give the same host-level visibility and control.
explanation.examTip: Licenses bound to sockets/cores = Dedicated Hosts.

stem: A company is comparing on-premises IT with AWS.
prompt: Which TWO are typical advantages of AWS? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Customers manage the physical security of data centers
options.why: Physical security is AWS's responsibility.

options.text: Hardware must be purchased three years in advance
options.why: That describes on-premises planning, not AWS.

options.text: Capacity can scale with demand
options.why: Elasticity lets capacity follow demand, so it meets the requirement described here.

options.text: Prices are fixed regardless of usage
options.why: AWS pricing is generally usage-based, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Resources can be provisioned in minutes
options.why: Self-service, on-demand provisioning gives speed and agility.

explanation.answer: AWS offers on-demand provisioning in minutes and elastic capacity that follows demand.
explanation.concept: These benefits come from self-service, API-driven infrastructure.
explanation.examTip: Fast provisioning + elastic scaling = classic AWS advantages.

stem: A news website based in Europe has many readers in Asia who complain about slow page loads.
prompt: Which approach BEST reduces latency for those readers?

options.text: Serve content through Amazon CloudFront edge locations
options.why: CloudFront caches content at edge locations near readers, lowering latency.

options.text: Increase the size of the web servers in Europe
options.why: Larger servers don't shorten the network distance to Asia.

options.text: Compress the database backups
options.why: Backup compression has no effect on page load times.

options.text: Add a second Availability Zone in the European Region
options.why: Another AZ in the same Region doesn't move content closer to Asia.

explanation.answer: Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network that caches content at edge locations worldwide.
explanation.concept: Global reach on AWS includes Regions for applications and edge locations for content delivery.
explanation.examTip: Distant users + slow pages = CloudFront.

stem: A company keeps 200 TB of compliance records that are rarely read but must be retained for seven years.
prompt: Which approach lowers storage cost the MOST?

options.text: Keep everything in Amazon S3 Standard
options.why: S3 Standard is designed for frequently accessed data and costs more for archives.

options.text: Move the records to an Amazon S3 Glacier storage class
options.why: Glacier storage classes are designed for low-cost, long-term archival storage.

options.text: Keep the records on premises on new hardware
options.why: Buying hardware adds capital cost and maintenance.

options.text: Store the records on EBS volumes attached to EC2
options.why: EBS is block storage priced for active use and costs more for archives.

explanation.answer: Amazon S3 Glacier storage classes provide very low-cost storage for data that is rarely accessed.
explanation.concept: Matching storage classes to access patterns is a key cost optimization practice.
explanation.examTip: Rarely accessed, keep for years = S3 Glacier storage classes.

stem: A company's security team asks how AWS can respond to new threats faster than most individual companies.
prompt: Which reason is MOST accurate?

options.text: AWS disables customer applications during threats
options.why: AWS does not disable customer applications to respond to threats.

options.text: AWS requires customers to install AWS antivirus software
options.why: There is no mandatory AWS antivirus for customers.

options.text: AWS sees signals across a global infrastructure at massive scale
options.why: Operating at scale gives AWS broad visibility and dedicated security teams.

options.text: AWS shares customers' private data to learn about threats
options.why: AWS does not use customers' private data this way.

explanation.answer: AWS operates at massive scale with dedicated security teams, which helps it detect and respond to threats across its infrastructure.
explanation.concept: Customers inherit the security controls AWS builds for the underlying infrastructure.
explanation.examTip: Scale = better visibility and specialized security teams for the infrastructure.

stem: During migration, a company moves its Java application from its own application servers to AWS Elastic Beanstalk with almost no code changes.
prompt: Which migration strategy is this?

options.text: Repurchase
options.why: Repurchasing replaces the application with a new product.

options.text: Retain
options.why: Retaining keeps the application on premises.

options.text: Refactor
options.why: Refactoring redesigns the application, which is not happening here.

options.text: Replatform
options.why: Moving to a managed platform with minimal changes is replatforming.

explanation.answer: Moving to a managed platform like Elastic Beanstalk, with few code changes, is a replatform migration.
explanation.concept: Replatforming gains some cloud benefits, such as less server management, without a rewrite.
explanation.examTip: Same app, new managed platform, minimal changes = replatform.

stem: A company's leadership is discussing cloud computing models.
prompt: Which model gives the customer the MOST control over the operating system and network settings?

options.text: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
options.why: IaaS, like Amazon EC2, provides servers, storage and networking that the customer configures.

options.text: Software as a service (SaaS)
options.why: SaaS delivers a finished application with very little infrastructure control.

options.text: Function as a service
options.why: Functions run on infrastructure fully managed by the provider.

options.text: Platform as a service (PaaS)
options.why: PaaS manages the operating system and platform for you.

explanation.answer: IaaS gives the highest level of flexibility and control over IT resources. PaaS and SaaS hand more management to the provider.
explanation.concept: Types of cloud computing: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
explanation.examTip: Most control = IaaS. Least management = SaaS.

stem: A development team wants to deploy web applications without managing the underlying operating systems, patches or capacity planning.
prompt: Which cloud computing model fits BEST?

options.text: Colocation
options.why: Colocation means managing your own hardware in a rented facility.

options.text: Platform as a service (PaaS)
options.why: PaaS removes the need to manage the underlying infrastructure so teams can focus on deploying applications.

options.text: On-premises virtualization
options.why: On premises, the team manages everything.

options.text: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
options.why: IaaS leaves operating system management to the customer.

explanation.answer: PaaS removes the need to manage underlying infrastructure (hardware and operating systems). AWS Elastic Beanstalk is an example.
explanation.concept: PaaS is a middle ground between IaaS control and SaaS simplicity.
explanation.examTip: Deploy code, don't manage OS = PaaS (e.g., Elastic Beanstalk).

stem: A company uses a web-based email service that the provider fully runs and maintains. Employees only use the application.
prompt: Which cloud computing model is this?

options.text: Hybrid cloud
options.why: Hybrid describes a deployment model, not a service model.

options.text: Platform as a service
options.why: PaaS would require deploying and managing your own application.

options.text: Software as a service (SaaS)
options.why: SaaS provides a complete product that is run and managed by the provider.

options.text: Infrastructure as a service
options.why: IaaS would require managing servers and operating systems.

explanation.answer: With SaaS, the provider runs and manages the whole application; customers just use it.
explanation.concept: Examples include web email and many business applications.
explanation.examTip: Just use the app = SaaS.

stem: A company has a steady baseline workload that runs 24/7 for the next three years, plus unpredictable short spikes.
prompt: Which pricing approach is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: On-Demand for everything to stay flexible
options.why: On-Demand is flexible but costs the most for steady 24/7 usage.

options.text: Dedicated Hosts for everything
options.why: Dedicated Hosts are for licensing or compliance needs and cost more.

options.text: Spot Instances for the baseline and spikes
options.why: Spot can be interrupted, which is risky for a steady baseline that must run.

options.text: Savings Plans for the baseline and On-Demand for spikes
options.why: Committing on the steady baseline earns a discount, while spikes stay flexible.

explanation.answer: Combining pricing models matches each part of a workload to the right price: commitments for steady use, On-Demand for unpredictable spikes.
explanation.concept: Common pattern: commit for the baseline, On-Demand or Spot above it.
explanation.examTip: Steady baseline + spikes = Savings Plan/RI for base + On-Demand for peaks.

stem: A team wants to compare three instance types under real load before choosing one for production.
prompt: Why is this easier on AWS than on premises?

options.text: You can launch each type briefly and pay only for the hours used
options.why: On-demand access makes short benchmarks cheap and fast.

options.text: AWS requires customers to test every instance type
options.why: There is no such requirement, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: On-premises servers can't run benchmarks
options.why: On-premises servers can, but buying three hardware types just to test is costly.

options.text: AWS discounts instances that are used for tests
options.why: Test instances are billed like any others.

explanation.answer: On AWS you can benchmark different instance types for a few hours each and keep only the best one.
explanation.concept: Experimenting more often is a performance efficiency design principle.
explanation.examTip: Cheap, quick experiments = on-demand access to many resource types.

stem: An AWS bill shows charges for unattached EBS volumes and Elastic IP addresses that nobody uses.
prompt: Which practice would prevent this waste?

options.text: Increase the size of the EBS volumes
options.why: Larger volumes cost more, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Regularly identify and delete unused resources
options.why: Cleaning up idle resources removes charges that bring no value.

options.text: Buy Reserved Instances for the unused resources
options.why: Reservations discount resources you use; they don't remove waste.

options.text: Move the resources to another Region
options.why: Moving unused resources still incurs charges.

explanation.answer: Unused resources still cost money. Regular cleanup, often using AWS Trusted Advisor or Cost Explorer insights, keeps costs down.
explanation.concept: Cost optimization is ongoing: find and remove idle and underused resources.
explanation.examTip: Paying for things nobody uses = find and delete idle resources.

stem: A manager asks what the reliability pillar is about.
prompt: Which answer is BEST?

options.text: Protecting data from unauthorized access
options.why: That describes security, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Making the workload as cheap as possible
options.why: That describes cost optimization, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Performing the intended function correctly and consistently
options.why: Reliability covers a workload doing what it should, when it should, and recovering from failures.

options.text: Reducing the carbon footprint of workloads
options.why: That describes sustainability, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: The reliability pillar covers the ability of a workload to perform its intended function correctly and consistently, including recovery from failure.
explanation.concept: Key areas include foundations, workload architecture, change management and failure management.
explanation.examTip: Correct, consistent, recovers = reliability.

stem: A company plans to move a large data warehouse to AWS while its reporting tools stay on premises and download huge result sets every day.
prompt: Which cost should the company review carefully before migrating?

options.text: The cost of using the AWS Management Console
options.why: The console is free to use, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: The cost of creating IAM users
options.why: IAM is offered at no additional charge, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Data transfer into AWS from the internet
options.why: Data transfer into AWS from the internet is generally free.

options.text: Data transfer out of AWS to the on-premises tools
options.why: Data transfer out to the internet or on premises is charged and can add up for large daily downloads.

explanation.answer: Data transfer out of AWS is billed per GB, so architectures that move large volumes out every day should be reviewed.
explanation.concept: Keeping consumers close to data, or using AWS Direct Connect, can reduce data transfer costs.
explanation.examTip: Inbound is usually free; outbound is charged.

stem: An architect is reviewing a workload against cloud design principles.
prompt: Which TWO changes follow AWS design best practices? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Hard-code server IP addresses into the application
options.why: Hard-coded IPs make components tightly coupled and hard to replace.

options.text: Turn off monitoring to reduce costs
options.why: Monitoring is essential for reliability and operations.

options.text: Replace a single large server with an Auto Scaling group across AZs
options.why: This removes a single point of failure and adds elasticity.

options.text: Configure each server by hand through SSH
options.why: Manual configuration causes drift and slow recovery.

options.text: Use a queue between the web tier and the processing tier
options.why: A queue decouples tiers so they scale and fail independently.

explanation.answer: Scaling horizontally across AZs and decoupling with queues are core design principles for reliable, scalable workloads.
explanation.concept: Other principles: automate, treat resources as disposable, and design for failure.
explanation.examTip: Good: horizontal scaling, multi-AZ, decoupling, automation. Bad: hard-coding, manual changes.
